title: a website is a cocoon for becoming
content:
more on digital ecosystems

last week, I shared the story of cocoonery — the first website home I inhabited at age 22, which, in retrospect, served as a digital cocoon to help me incubate and discover my personal creative process. I’ve been writing about the idea of “website as cocoon” — first, in my recent iteration of house on the webs course.

today, I wanted to expand on what I mean by this metaphor.

a website is first (and always) a cocoon

a website must be, first, a cocoon — before it becomes its own world.

then, it must always still be a cocoon for the creator — even after it’s existed and matured for five or ten years — because to be a cocoon space is to feel safe to be always in process. to keep a web world truly alive is to embody its ongoingness.


a website as cocoon is:
a semi-public internet vessel where you feel both safe and free to explore, dream, and process your ideas/creativity — in an ongoing way.

it’s in cocooning containers that we give ourselves full permission to be soupy, incubative, and vulnerable. (and not a performative vulnerability with ulterior motives of getting attention or validation). a cocoon is inward-facing — first and foremost. there is a chaos, a tenderness, a spontaneity that comes with this space. you give yourself complete and total permission to be — and, at the same time, to be seen in the messiness of being.

a cocoon is nothing — if not the tender membrane around process.

a cocoon is for gathering resources

a web cocoon is, above all, an intention — rather than a specific shape, design, or output. it’s important that the container must support the intention. you cannot have a cocoon in a hostile environment, or in a carefully designed place where the system’s motives are misaligned with yours.

that is to say: I’m skeptical of using social platforms as cocoons — even if your account is private and no one follows you. community is not the problem; the problem is that the system itself is designed to exploit your inner, psychic resources.

a web cocoon is for exactly for that — for nourishing and gathering your inner resources. your attention and the capacity for focused, deep creation is one of the most precious resources that exist.

being in public, not performing

maybe you’re wondering: why can’t I keep it all private, like a folder on my desktop, or a writing app, or a Notion database in the comfort of my computer? those are certainly creative cocoons — and I highly encourage an abundance of them — but they are not the same as web cocoons.

web cocoons require you to be yourself in the public space — where we’ve been trained to perform, narrative, and compete for scarce resources. web cocoons must exist in a web — in relation to other real human souls. a folder in your desktop or a creative journal cannot trigger vulnerability in the same way that releasing oneself in the online world does. this vulnerability represents a growth edge. it grapples with the questions:

  • how can I be truly myself, in relation to the world — rather than performing narratives/scripted versions of myself?

  • how do I define myself, and my creative practice, and take accountability for who I am, in an ongoing way?


(for more on why sharing matters — see sharing your work as creative release)

a place for process and becoming

a website as cocoon is alive, soupy, messy — even after it is deliberately cultivated, structured, and thoughtfully designed. even after a website has matured into a rich, developed world of its own, with its own logic and ecosystem, it still remains a cocoon — as long as process remains an integral part of its identity.

process — like the creative seasons or inner weather — is always changing. process is always pushing the boundaries between what you’ve found to be true, and what you’re willing to experiment with, take a risk on, and surrender to. this is like having your two feet planted in the earth, and your eyes and hands stretched towards the cosmos.

when you decide that your website will be a cocoon, you decide to allow it to become a space, a vessel, a rainbow bridge for change, for meeting your future selves — without exactly knowing what forms you’ll metamorphosize into on the other side.
